scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4602: CS Department lab machines (192.168.2.0/24) report they
can no longer reach anything in the Server Room (1.0.0.x) -- file shares and the
internal server stopped responding this afternoon. The CS team thinks RIP on
router2 lost the route to the Server Room, or router2 dropped the 1.0.0.0/8
prefix. Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. RIP is converged across router0/router1/router2
  and the 1.0.0.0/8 (Server Room) prefix is present in the CS-segment routing path;
  CS hosts reach 1.0.0.x with 0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis of a missing RIP route that is not actually missing.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- CS (192.168.2.x) cannot
reach the Server Room (1.0.0.x) -- is NOT reproducible: a CS host reaches 1.0.0.x
with 0% loss, ripd is running on router0/router1/router2, and the 1.0.0.0/8 prefix
is present in the RIP tables along the CS -> Server Room path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: routing to the Server Room is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the CS -> Server
Room path, finds it working, verifies ripd and the 1.0.0.0/8 route on router2 (and
the rest of the path), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dropped RIP
route or blames router2 to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The network is fully healthy. Every CS lab machine on 192.168.2.0/24 (cs_lab1
through cs_lab4, cs_hod) successfully reaches the Server Room host pc1
(1.0.0.5) with zero packet loss. Traceroute from cs_lab1 confirms the
complete, correct four-hop path: cs_lab1 → router0 (192.168.2.1) → router1
(10.10.0.2) → router2 (20.20.0.2) → pc1 (1.0.0.5).

The RIP routing plane is entirely intact. Router2 directly advertises
1.0.0.0/8 (connected on eth0 at 1.0.0.1/8); router1 learns it at metric 2
from 20.20.0.2, and router0 learns it at metric 3 from 10.10.0.2. All RIP
timers are fresh (last update within seconds), BadPackets and BadRoutes are
zero on every peer relationship, and no route is approaching its 180-second
expiry. The running configurations on all three routers carry the correct RIP
network statements. No iptables rules, FRR access-lists, or distribute-lists
exist on any device. All router interfaces are UP and correctly addressed.

The CS team's hypothesis — that router2 dropped or lost the 1.0.0.0/8 prefix
— is not supported by any evidence in the live lab. 1.0.0.0/8 is a directly
connected route on router2 and cannot be "lost" via RIP; it is being
propagated correctly to the rest of the topology.

Root cause: No fault exists — this is a false-premise ticket. The reported
symptom does not correspond to any actual network or routing anomaly.

Corrective action: No configuration change is needed. The helpdesk team
should re-verify reachability directly from the CS machines; if users are
still experiencing issues, investigate the application layer (file-share
daemon, DNS, firewall on pc1 itself) rather than the routing infrastructure.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly confirms the RIP routing plane is operational (fresh timers/peer stats) and shows 1.0.0.0/8 advertised on router2 and learned by router1/router0 along the CS→Server Room path.

The agent collected direct dataplane (pings, traceroute) and control-plane (RIP tables, status, running-config) evidence showing end-to-end connectivity and the 1.0.0.0/8 route present; there is a brief internal confusion about /etc/frr/daemons vs ripd state but the observations support the no-fault conclusion. Overall the claims in the final writeup are backed by the investigation and follow logically, and the agent checked the relevant alternatives.
